subject: Mixed (Real Weightage)
description: 100 questions following the real PGP-CET 2025 subject weightage. Mix: 0 easy / 7 medium / 93 hard. Tier is relative: the hard third of the 60 papers by average question difficulty. Every question cites its source.

questions.question: Proprioception and vibration sense are carried in the:
questions.explanation: Dorsal columns: fine touch, vibration, proprioception (ipsilateral until the medulla). Spinothalamic: pain and temperature (contralateral).
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: A Bennett fracture is a:

options.B: Fracture of the neck of the fifth metacarpal
options.C: Fracture-dislocation of the base of the first metacarpal

questions.explanation: Intra-articular fracture-subluxation of the thumb CMC joint; the abductor pollicis longus displaces the shaft.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 4 Orthopedics)
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Which tissue absorbs ultrasound energy MOST per unit thickness?

options.D: Bone and other tissues rich in collagen and protein

questions.explanation: Absorption is highest in tissues with high protein/collagen content such as bone, tendon and ligament; lowest in fluid and fat.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Although prolactin levels are high throughout pregnancy, actual milk secretion does not begin until around the 3rd-4th postpartum day. What explains this delay?

options.A: Prolactin has no role in milk secretion at all
options.B: High circulating estrogen and progesterone during pregnancy make breast tissue unresponsive to prolactin; their withdrawal after delivery allows prolactin to act
options.C: The breasts are not anatomically ready until several days after birth
options.D: Oxytocin blocks prolactin receptors until labour is complete

questions.explanation: During pregnancy, the high circulating levels of estrogen and progesterone keep the fully-developed mammary glands unresponsive to prolactin, holding milk secretion in abeyance despite high prolactin levels. Once these steroids fall sharply after delivery, prolactin is free to begin its secretory (lactogenic) action.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Physiology of Lactation, Lactogenesis
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: A 95% confidence interval for a mean means that:

options.A: If the study were repeated many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true population mean
options.C: The true mean has a 95% probability of being in any single interval after it has been calculated, with certainty
options.D: 95% of individual observations lie within it

questions.explanation: CI reflects precision of the estimate; if a CI for a difference excludes 0 (or ratio excludes 1) the result is significant at 5%.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine; WHO/ICF and CBR guidelines; standard biostatistics/research methodology texts (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 6 Research and Analysis)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Which aquatic activity is MOST effective in reducing tone in a patient with spasticity?

options.C: Slow, passive movements with the patient floating supported in warm water

questions.explanation: Warm water, buoyancy and slow rhythmic movements relax muscles; speed and cold increase tone.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques; Dena Gardiner, Principles of Exercise Therapy; Tidy's Physiotherapy (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: A diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS) requires evidence of CNS damage that satisfies which two key criteria?

options.A: Damage in only one CNS location, confirmed once
options.B: Dissemination of lesions in space (at least two separate CNS areas) AND dissemination in time (damage at two separate points at least 1 month apart)
options.C: A single MRI scan showing any abnormality
options.D: Positive family history alone, without any imaging

questions.explanation: MS diagnosis requires evidence of damage in at least two separate areas of the CNS (dissemination in space) occurring at two separate points in time at least 1 month apart (dissemination in time), plus exclusion of other possible diagnoses — as reflected in the revised McDonald Criteria.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Which muscles form the pes anserinus at the medial tibia?
questions.explanation: Mnemonic: Say Grace before Tea.
questions.sourceBook: B.D. Chaurasia's Human Anatomy (Upper Limb, Lower Limb, Thorax, Head & Neck, Neuroanatomy) — chapter-level reference
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: The Jakob test (reverse pivot shift maneuver) is used to assess for which type of knee instability?

options.C: Isolated medial collateral ligament sprain only

questions.explanation: The Jakob test (reverse pivot shift maneuver) tests for posterolateral rotary instability — a positive test (jerk in the knee, or posterior tibial shift with a 'giving way' sensation) indicates injury to the lateral collateral ligament, arcuate-popliteus complex, and mid-third of the lateral capsule.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Tests for Posterolateral Rotary Instability
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: In acute respiratory distress syndrome, a key supportive position that improves oxygenation is:
questions.explanation: Prone positioning recruits dorsal lung regions and improves V/Q matching; used for at least 12–16 hours/day in severe ARDS.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems; ACSM Guidelines; Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: The earliest visible change in osteoarthritic cartilage is:

options.C: Fibrillation (surface irregularity) of the articular cartilage

questions.explanation: Early OA: loss of proteoglycan and surface fibrillation, followed by cartilage thinning, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes and cysts.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: When naming a peptide, the amino acid suffixes (e.g. '-ine' in glycine) are changed to '-yl' for every residue EXCEPT which one?

options.C: Any residue in the middle of the chain

questions.explanation: In peptide nomenclature, every amino acid's suffix is changed to '-yl' except the C-terminal residue, which keeps its normal name. For example, a tripeptide of glutamate-cysteine-glycine (glycine being C-terminal) is named glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine.
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Peptide Bond
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: Clarke's sign and the McConnell test are both special tests associated with which condition?
questions.explanation: Clarke's sign and the McConnell test are both used in the assessment of patellofemoral syndrome (anterior knee pain related to patellar tracking/compression issues).
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Special Tests Commonly Performed on the Knee

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When a MOTOR nerve is electrically stimulated, why does only the downward-travelling (efferent) impulse produce a muscle contraction, while the upward-travelling impulse has no motor effect?

options.A: The upward-travelling impulse is unable to pass the first synapse, since it is travelling in the wrong (antidromic) direction
options.B: The upward-travelling impulse travels faster and arrives too early to have any effect
options.C: Motor nerves cannot conduct impulses in more than one direction under any circumstance
options.D: Only the upward-travelling impulse reaches the muscle

questions.explanation: Stimulating a nerve fibre initiates impulses travelling simultaneously in both directions from the stimulation point. For a motor nerve, the upward (antidromic) impulse cannot pass the first synapse it encounters travelling the 'wrong' way, so it has no effect, while the downward (orthodromic) impulse reaches the muscle normally and causes contraction.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Nerve Stimulation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: A cervical rib may cause thoracic outlet syndrome by compressing the:

options.A: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus
options.D: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1) and subclavian artery

questions.explanation: Wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles and Raynaud-like symptoms.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 4 Orthopedics)
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Population inversion in laser physics refers to a state in which:

options.A: More electrons are in the ground state than in the excited state
options.B: The medium is at absolute zero
options.C: More electrons are in an excited (metastable) state than in the ground state
options.D: All electrons are removed from the atom

questions.explanation: Population inversion is required for stimulated emission to exceed absorption and thereby amplify light.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: During full elevation of the arm the clavicle:

options.D: Rotates posteriorly about its long axis by about 30–50°

questions.explanation: Posterior rotation of the clavicle allows the scapula to upwardly rotate and permits complete elevation.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Neumann, Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System; Daniels & Worthingham (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 3 Biomechanics)
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: When treating a patient with dementia the therapist should:

options.D: Use simple short instructions, a consistent routine and demonstration

questions.explanation: Cognitive impairment limits learning of new skills; use demonstration, repetition and familiar tasks.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems; ACSM Guidelines; Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Why do medium-frequency currents pass through the skin more comfortably than low-frequency currents?

options.B: Skin capacitive reactance falls as frequency rises, so skin impedance is lower
options.C: They are not conducted by nerves at all
options.D: Skin resistance rises as frequency rises

questions.explanation: Skin behaves partly as a capacitor. Capacitive reactance = 1/(2πfC), so at higher frequencies the impedance is lower and more current penetrates with less discomfort at the skin.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: To increase lateral rotation of the glenohumeral joint, the humeral head should be mobilised with:
questions.explanation: Convex–concave rule: humeral head (convex) on glenoid (concave); the head glides in the direction opposite to the bone motion. Lateral rotation needs anterior glide; medial rotation needs posterior glide.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: In the 'ischemic penumbra' surrounding the core of an acute ischemic stroke, neurons:

options.A: Die immediately within seconds, identical to the ischemic core
options.B: Survive for a somewhat longer period than core neurons, but will die without timely reperfusion — making this tissue a key target for acute treatment
options.C: Are completely unaffected by the stroke

questions.explanation: While neurons in the ischemic core die within minutes, the surrounding penumbra contains neurons that survive somewhat longer but remain at risk — cell survival depends on the severity and duration of ischemia, and without timely reperfusion, cells in the penumbra will die and the infarct will expand. This makes the penumbra the key target of emergency stroke treatment.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Plyometric exercise is based on the principle that:

options.A: A rapid eccentric stretch of a muscle before a concentric contraction increases the force of the subsequent contraction
options.C: Resistance should be applied only in one direction
options.D: A slow stretch reduces the stretch reflex

questions.explanation: Stretch–shortening cycle uses elastic energy and the stretch reflex; used in late-stage rehabilitation (jumping, bounding).
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques; Dena Gardiner, Principles of Exercise Therapy; Tidy's Physiotherapy (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: The pain of acute pericarditis is typically:

options.A: Crushing and radiating to the left arm with exertion
options.D: Sharp, pleuritic, relieved by sitting forward

questions.explanation: A pericardial friction rub may be heard.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference); standard internal medicine texts
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: In Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), what is emphasised as more diagnostically useful than the radiographic appearance alone?

options.A: The timing of the radiographic changes relative to the insult and onset of symptoms
options.C: The exact colour of the consolidation on the film
options.D: The time of day the X-ray was taken

questions.explanation: In ARDS, it is the TIMING of radiographic changes relative to the inciting insult and the onset of clinical symptoms — rather than the radiological appearance alone (which resembles pulmonary oedema) — that helps suggest the diagnosis, since the chest radiograph is often normal in the initial hours despite clinical distress.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Thoracic Imaging — Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: A drug that reacts with an enzyme's catalytic site so strongly (via a covalent bond or very high affinity) that the normal substrate cannot displace it produces which kinetic pattern?

options.A: kM unchanged, Vmax unchanged (no real inhibition)
options.C: kM increased and Vmax reduced — a non-equilibrium type of competitive inhibition
options.D: Only Vmax changes while kM decreases proportionally

questions.explanation: Classical competitive inhibition (equilibrium type) raises kM but leaves Vmax unchanged, since enough substrate can still out-compete the inhibitor. But when the inhibitor binds essentially irreversibly at the same catalytic site (e.g. organophosphates on cholinesterase, or methotrexate's very high affinity for dihydrofolate reductase), substrate can no longer displace it — this non-equilibrium type raises kM AND reduces Vmax.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: Rood's approach to neurological rehabilitation primarily uses:

options.A: Sensory stimulation (brushing, icing, tapping) to influence muscle tone

questions.explanation: Rood used cutaneous stimulation (quick brushing, icing, stroking), proprioceptive stimuli and ontogenetic sequence of postural patterns.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Cerebral edema following ischemic stroke typically reaches its maximum at approximately what time point, and is the most frequent cause of death in acute stroke?
questions.explanation: Cerebral edema begins within minutes of the ischemic insult and reaches its maximum by 3 to 4 days, gradually subsiding by 2 to 3 weeks. Significant edema, particularly with large MCA/ICA infarcts, is the most frequent cause of death in acute stroke due to raised intracranial pressure and brainstem herniation.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: The hip strategy for balance recovery is typically used when:

options.B: Perturbation is large or the support surface is narrow, requiring rapid movement at the hips
options.D: A small slow sway is controlled at the ankle

questions.explanation: Ankle strategy handles small perturbations on firm ground; hip strategy is for larger/faster ones; stepping strategy for the largest.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques; Dena Gardiner, Principles of Exercise Therapy; Tidy's Physiotherapy (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: Charcot's triad of multiple sclerosis consists of:

options.C: Nystagmus, intention tremor and scanning speech

questions.explanation: Reflects brainstem/cerebellar involvement: nystagmus, intention tremor, scanning (staccato) speech.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Coeliac disease is a hypersensitivity to:
questions.explanation: Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies; villous atrophy on biopsy.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference); standard internal medicine texts
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: In fat necrosis due to acute pancreatitis, free fatty acids released from ruptured adipocytes combine with calcium to form:
questions.explanation: In fat necrosis, liberated pancreatic lipases cause hydrolysis of adipocytes, releasing free fatty acids which complex with calcium to form calcium soaps — a process called saponification, giving the necrotic foci their firm, chalky-white gross appearance.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Fat Necrosis
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: BCR-ABL fusion; treated with imatinib.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference); standard internal medicine texts
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: Which advice following total hip replacement is INCORRECT?

options.A: Keep a pillow between your legs while sleeping
options.C: When turning, pivot on the operated leg

questions.explanation: Pivoting on the operated leg combines rotation and adduction with the foot fixed and risks dislocation. Patients should take small steps to turn.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Why is the metaphysis of a growing long bone especially important clinically when it lies partly within a joint capsule?

options.A: It has no blood supply, so infection cannot spread there at all
options.B: Being an actively growing, richly vascularised part of the bone, infection there can spread into the joint if the metaphysis is intracapsular (and vice versa)
options.C: It is always extracapsular in every long bone, so it never affects joints
options.D: It only matters in the lower limb, not the upper limb

questions.explanation: The metaphysis is the actively growing part of the bone adjacent to the epiphyseal line, with a rich blood supply — making it a common site for infection in young people. Where the metaphysis is partly or wholly intracapsular (as at the upper end of the humerus), joint infection can spread to the metaphysis, and metaphyseal disease can spread into the joint.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Capsular Attachments and Epiphyseal Lines
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: Which treatment is inappropriate during an acute flare of rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.explanation: Acute inflammation calls for rest, gentle range of motion and pain relief; stretching/mobilisation aggravates synovitis.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems; ACSM Guidelines; Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: After a fracture of both the radius and ulna shafts, why must cross-union (bony union between the two bones) be specifically prevented during healing?

options.B: Cross-union would permanently fuse the radius and ulna together, abolishing pronation and supination of the hand
options.C: Cross-union only affects elbow flexion, not the hand
options.D: It increases the risk of scaphoid fracture

questions.explanation: Pronation and supination depend on the radius being able to rotate around a stable ulna. If the two bones heal fused together (cross-union), that rotation becomes impossible, so surgeons take specific care during fixation of combined radius-ulna shaft fractures to prevent it.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Clinical Anatomy
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: Edman's reagent (phenylisothiocyanate) is used in protein sequencing chiefly because it allows:

options.A: Complete hydrolysis of the protein into free amino acids only
options.B: Selective labelling and removal of the N-terminal amino acid as a PTH-derivative, leaving the rest of the polypeptide intact for repeated cycles
options.C: Cleavage of the protein only at cysteine residues
options.D: Permanent, irreversible denaturation of all peptide bonds

questions.explanation: Unlike Sanger's reagent (which labels and then requires full hydrolysis, destroying the polypeptide), Edman's reagent selectively removes and identifies the N-terminal amino acid as a phenylthiohydantoin (PTH) derivative while leaving the remaining polypeptide intact — allowing the process to be repeated cycle after cycle to read the sequence progressively.
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Determination of Primary Structure
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: The Neer and Hawkins–Kennedy tests are used to detect:
questions.explanation: Passive forced flexion (Neer) or flexion with medial rotation at 90° (Hawkins) squeezes the supraspinatus against the coracoacromial arch.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: The commonest type of breech presentation is:
questions.explanation: The buttocks present with hips flexed and knees extended.
questions.sourceBook: D.C. Dutta, Textbook of Obstetrics and Textbook of Gynaecology (chapter-level reference)
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: True phimosis, as distinguished from a normal non-retractile foreskin in a young boy, is characterised by:

options.A: Simple inability to retract the foreskin at age 2, which is entirely normal
options.B: Whitish scarring of the foreskin caused by balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO), rarely seen before age 5
options.C: Ballooning of the foreskin during urination with no scarring
options.D: A condition that always requires surgery in infancy

questions.explanation: 'Phimosis' is often wrongly applied to a normal non-retractile foreskin, which is common and physiological in young boys. True phimosis is pathological whitish scarring caused by balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO), and is rare before 5 years of age.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — The Foreskin and Circumcision
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Hip subluxation in spastic cerebral palsy is most commonly due to spasm of the:
questions.explanation: Adductor and iliopsoas tightness with weak abductors lead to hip migration; surveillance with pelvic X-ray is routine.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: The tenodesis action in the hand means that:

options.B: Wrist flexion causes active finger extension
options.C: Wrist extension causes passive finger flexion by tension in the finger flexor tendons

questions.explanation: Used functionally in C6 tetraplegia; finger flexor tendon shortening should therefore not be stretched.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Neumann, Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System; Daniels & Worthingham (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 3 Biomechanics)
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Morning headaches in a patient with severe respiratory failure may signify:

options.C: Normal sleep patterns with no pathology

questions.explanation: Morning headaches in patients with severe respiratory failure may signify nocturnal carbon dioxide retention (hypercapnia during sleep), which can be confirmed with early morning arterial blood gases or nocturnal transcutaneous CO2 monitoring.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a second-class lever in the body?

options.C: Elevating the arm with the deltoid

questions.explanation: Calf muscle effort is at the heel (calcaneus) with the resistance (body weight through the tibia) lying between the axis (toes) and the effort.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Neumann, Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System; Daniels & Worthingham (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 3 Biomechanics)

questions.question: Which of the following is cited as a genuine limitation of mortality data, particularly relevant to developing countries like India?

options.A: Incomplete reporting of deaths and lack of accuracy in recording age/cause of death
options.B: Mortality data is always 100% complete and accurate worldwide
options.C: Death certificates do not exist in any country
options.D: Mortality data cannot be tabulated by any coding system

questions.explanation: Incomplete reporting of deaths is not usually a problem in developed countries, but can be considerable in India and other developing countries. Combined with inaccuracies in age/cause recording (often due to lack of diagnostic evidence, inexperienced certifying doctors, or absence of postmortem examination), this is a genuine limitation of mortality data quality.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — Limitations of Mortality Data
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: A choke coil (inductor) in a circuit mainly:

options.A: Opposes rapid changes in current, allowing low-frequency/steady current but impeding high-frequency alternating current
options.B: Blocks direct current and passes only high frequencies

questions.explanation: An inductor's reactance rises with frequency (X = 2πfL), so it smooths current and attenuates high-frequency components.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: A valgus stress applied to the knee at 30° of flexion tests the:
questions.explanation: Valgus stress opens the medial side; varus stress tests the lateral collateral ligament.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: The latent period between UV exposure and the appearance of erythema is:

options.A: Longer for UVA than for UVB; typically about 2–8 hours (UVB)
options.B: Longer for a higher dose in every case

questions.explanation: UVB erythema appears after a latent period of about 1.5–8 h, peaks at 12–24 h, and the greater the dose the shorter the latent period.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Within the femoral sheath, which compartment contains the femoral canal (occupied by a lymph node), and which structure occupies the intermediate compartment?

options.A: The medial compartment is the femoral canal; the femoral vein occupies the intermediate compartment
options.B: The lateral compartment is the femoral canal; the femoral artery occupies the intermediate compartment
options.C: The femoral nerve occupies the femoral canal
options.D: There is only one compartment in the femoral sheath

questions.explanation: The femoral sheath has three compartments: the lateral compartment contains the femoral artery, the intermediate compartment contains the femoral vein, and the medial compartment is the femoral canal, occupied by a lymph node (and providing space for femoral vein distension, and the path for femoral hernias).
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Lower Limb
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: The most reliable early clinical sign of compartment syndrome is:

options.C: Pain out of proportion to the injury, worsened by passive stretch of the muscles in the compartment

questions.explanation: Pain on passive stretch is the earliest sign. Pulselessness, pallor and paralysis are late; diagnosis is clinical, with pressure measurement when uncertain.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Muscle energy technique (MET) uses:

options.A: The patient's own isometric contraction against a counterforce, followed by relaxation and stretch

questions.explanation: MET (Mitchell): patient contracts a muscle isometrically against a controlled counterforce (post-isometric relaxation), then the therapist takes up the new barrier.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: For a RISING (increasing) current applied over a superficial nerve, which electrode is more effective at initiating a nerve impulse, and why is the active electrode typically connected to it?

options.A: The anode, because it requires less current overall
options.B: The cathode, because it produces contraction of innervated muscle with less current than is required at the anode
options.C: Neither electrode has any different effect
options.D: The anode always requires less current than the cathode

questions.explanation: For a rising current, the cathode is more effective at initiating a nerve impulse than the anode. This is why the active electrode is conventionally connected to the cathode — it produces contraction of innervated muscle using less current than would be needed if the anode were used as the active electrode.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Mechanism of Nerve Stimulation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: In epidemiological terminology, a 'variate' that can only be present or absent (e.g. lung cancer, a broken leg) is described as:

options.D: Non-measurable and therefore not usable in epidemiology

questions.explanation: A variate (any piece of information about a patient or their disease) can be discrete — present or absent, like lung cancer or a broken leg — or continuously distributed, like blood pressure, serum cholesterol, or height. A 'circumstance' is a distinct concept: any environmental factor suspected of causing a disease, such as air pollution.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Epidemiology and Epidemiologic Methods — Basic Measurements in Epidemiology
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Plasmodium falciparum causes markedly more severe (malignant) malaria than the other three plasmodial species mainly because:

options.A: It has an exo-erythrocytic stage that the others lack
options.B: It only infects the liver, never red blood cells
options.C: It parasitises red cells of any age, can infect a single red cell multiple times, and makes parasitised red cells sticky, causing capillary obstruction in deep organs
options.D: It is transmitted by a different mosquito genus entirely

questions.explanation: Unlike the other plasmodial species (which parasitise only juvenile red cells and lack these features), P. falciparum parasitises red cells of any age, can infect a single red cell with more than one parasite, and makes infected red cells sticky — causing capillary obstruction (e.g. in the brain, producing cerebral malaria) that accounts for its exceptional virulence. It also notably lacks an exo-erythrocytic stage, but that is not the source of its severity.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: The length of the near field (Fresnel zone) of an ultrasound beam increases when:

options.C: The transducer radius is larger or the wavelength is shorter (higher frequency)

questions.explanation: Near-field length = r²/λ. Within the near field the beam is highly irregular; the far field is more uniform and divergent.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: 'Physical dependence' on a drug is best defined as:

options.A: Simply enjoying the effects of a drug with no physiological consequence of stopping it
options.B: An altered physiological state (neuroadaptation) requiring the continued presence of the drug to maintain equilibrium, such that stopping it produces a characteristic withdrawal syndrome
options.C: A purely psychological craving with no biological basis whatsoever
options.D: A condition seen only with stimulant drugs like cocaine and amphetamines

questions.explanation: Physical dependence is an altered physiological state produced by repeated drug administration, requiring the drug's continued presence to maintain equilibrium ('neuroadaptation'); stopping the drug produces a characteristic withdrawal syndrome. Drugs like opioids, barbiturates, alcohol, and benzodiazepines produce physical dependence, while stimulants like amphetamines and cocaine produce little or none, despite being highly reinforcing.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognised physical complication of a severe, chronic cough?
questions.explanation: Chronic, forceful coughing can cause 'cough fractures' of the ribs and hernias, due to the repeated high intra-thoracic and intra-abdominal pressures generated. Stress urinary incontinence is another common, often under-reported complication, especially in women.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Infarcts of the lung, intestine and liver are typically:
questions.explanation: Pale infarcts occur in solid organs with end-arterial supply: heart, kidney, spleen.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology; Ananthanarayan & Paniker, Textbook of Microbiology (chapter-level reference)
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: In managing spasticity in MS patients, why must a therapist be cautious about excessive pharmacological reduction of spasticity in some patients?

options.A: Spasticity has no functional role and should always be eliminated completely
options.B: Spasticity can sometimes be functionally useful (e.g. extensor spasticity assisting standing during a stand-pivot transfer), so over-reducing it may cause loss of function
options.C: Antispasticity medications have no side effects to worry about
options.D: Spasticity always improves function no matter how severe

questions.explanation: While excessive spasticity impairs function, spasticity can sometimes substitute for lost strength — for example, extensor spasticity assisting a patient during a stand-pivot transfer. Significant pharmacological reduction of spasticity in such cases could therefore paradoxically worsen functional performance.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 16: Multiple Sclerosis — Management of Symptoms, Spasticity
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Permanent hardness of water is due to the presence of:

options.D: Sulphates and chlorides of calcium and magnesium

questions.explanation: Temporary hardness (bicarbonates) is removed by boiling.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine; WHO/ICF and CBR guidelines; standard biostatistics/research methodology texts (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 6 Research and Analysis)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Acetic acid iontophoresis for calcific tendinitis relies on delivering which ion?
questions.explanation: Acetate is an anion; like charges repel, so it is driven into tissue from the cathode, where it may help dissolve calcium deposits.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Which finding would NOT be expected with a C6 root lesion?

options.A: Paraesthesia of the middle and ring fingers
options.B: Sensory loss over the thumb and lateral forearm
options.D: Weakness of biceps and wrist extensors

questions.explanation: C6 root: thumb/index sensory loss, biceps and wrist extension weakness; the middle finger is C7 and ring/little C8.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: In the first week postpartum, there is a secondary increase in fibrinogen, factor VIII, and platelets. What clinical risk does this hypercoagulable state primarily raise?
questions.explanation: The secondary rise in fibrinogen, factor VIII, and platelet count (with increased platelet adhesiveness) during the first postpartum week increases the risk of thrombosis — one reason early ambulation and postpartum exercise are actively encouraged, since enhanced fibrinolytic activity in the first few days acts as a partial protective counter-mechanism.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Intradiscal pressure of the lumbar spine is HIGHEST in:

options.A: Sitting while leaning forward with a load

questions.explanation: Nachemson: supine 25%, side-lying 75%, standing 100%, sitting 140%, sitting flexed with load 275%.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Neumann, Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System; Daniels & Worthingham (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 3 Biomechanics)
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: The Y-BOCS, a widely used clinical scale for OCD, stands for and is used to:

options.A: Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale — elicit symptoms and rate severity of OCD
options.B: Young-Beck Obsessive Cognition Scale — diagnose depression only
options.C: Yale Behavioural Outcome Classification System — used only in research, never clinically
options.D: A scale exclusively for measuring anxiety, unrelated to OCD

questions.explanation: Y-BOCS stands for the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale, one of the most useful clinical tools for eliciting the range of obsessive and compulsive symptoms present and rating the overall severity of OCD.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: Maximum coronary blood flow to the left ventricle occurs during:
questions.explanation: During systole intramyocardial pressure compresses the coronary vessels.
questions.sourceBook: A.K. Jain, Textbook of Physiology; Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology (chapter-level reference)
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: An ABG shows pH 7.30, PaCO2 60 mmHg and normal bicarbonate. This is:
questions.explanation: Low pH with high PaCO2 and normal HCO3⁻ indicates uncompensated respiratory acidosis (e.g. acute ventilatory failure).
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems; ACSM Guidelines; Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Moon face, central obesity, purple striae and hypertension suggest:
questions.explanation: Commonest cause is exogenous glucocorticoids; Addison's disease causes hypotension and pigmentation.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference); standard internal medicine texts
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: A stroke patient has nonfluent, slow, hesitant speech with a limited vocabulary, but relatively preserved auditory comprehension. This is classically associated with a lesion of:

options.A: Wernicke's area, in the posterior temporal gyrus
options.B: Broca's area, in the third frontal convolution of the dominant hemisphere

questions.explanation: This is classic Broca's (nonfluent, expressive) aphasia — slow, effortful, nonfluent speech with a limited vocabulary but relatively preserved comprehension — caused by a lesion of Broca's area in the dominant (typically left) frontal lobe. Wernicke's (fluent, receptive) aphasia, by contrast, produces fluent but often meaningless speech with impaired comprehension.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Middle Cerebral Artery Syndrome
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia and past-pointing are signs of:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar dysfunction produces ipsilateral incoordination; Parkinson's gives resting tremor with rigidity.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: Bronchiolitis in infants is usually caused by:
questions.explanation: RSV causes small airway inflammation with wheeze; treatment is supportive.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems; ACSM Guidelines; Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: During a maximum-effort CONCENTRIC muscle contraction, what happens to the force a muscle can generate as the velocity of shortening increases?

options.B: Force decreases as the velocity of muscle shortening increases
options.C: Force remains completely constant regardless of velocity
options.D: Force becomes unmeasurable at any velocity above zero

questions.explanation: For a maximal concentric contraction, force output decreases as the velocity of muscle shortening increases — the muscle has less time to develop peak tension at higher shortening velocities. This is opposite to the pattern often seen with eccentric contractions, where force initially rises with velocity before leveling off.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: A 'pseudomyostatic' (apparent) contracture, as distinguished from a true myostatic contracture, is primarily caused by:

options.A: An actual reduction in the number of sarcomeres arranged in series within the muscle
options.B: Hypertonicity such as spasticity or rigidity following a CNS lesion, which can be temporarily reduced with neuromuscular inhibition techniques
options.D: Replacement of normal muscle tissue with fibrotic scar tissue

questions.explanation: Unlike a true myostatic contracture (adaptive shortening of the muscle-tendon unit itself with no specific muscle pathology), a pseudomyostatic contracture results from ongoing hypertonicity, muscle spasm, or pain — the muscle only appears shortened, and full passive elongation becomes possible again once inhibition techniques temporarily reduce that muscle tension.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 4: Stretching for Impaired Mobility — Types of Contracture
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: A hamartoma is best defined as:

options.A: A malignant tumour of embryonal blastema seen mainly in infants
options.B: A benign tumour composed of mature but disorganised cells/tissues that are normally indigenous to that organ
options.C: An ectopic island of otherwise completely normal tissue in the wrong location
options.D: A tumour combining epithelial and mesenchymal malignant elements

questions.explanation: A hamartoma is a benign lesion made up of mature, differentiated tissue elements that are normal to the organ in question, just disorganised/jumbled — e.g. a pulmonary hamartoma contains mature cartilage, smooth muscle, and epithelium, all normal bronchial components arranged abnormally. This is distinct from a choristoma (ectopic normal tissue in the wrong site) and from blastomas (embryonal tumours of children).
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: A hallmark intellectual deficit seen after prefrontal-lobe damage, distinct from a general drop in IQ (which is often unaffected), is:

options.A: Complete loss of the ability to speak
options.B: Difficulty planning and sequencing actions, plus perseveration (continuing a behaviour even when the situation demands a new response)
options.D: Immediate loss of all long-term memories formed before the injury

questions.explanation: While standard IQ tests are often little affected by prefrontal damage, patients show subtle but characteristic deficits: difficulty planning a sequence of actions, and perseveration — a tendency to keep behaving the same way even when circumstances call for a different response.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Frontal-Lobe Association Cortex
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: The physiological basis of hold-relax stretching is:

options.D: Autogenic inhibition via Golgi tendon organs after an isometric contraction

questions.explanation: A maximal isometric contraction of the shortened muscle stimulates GTOs, followed by relaxation and a deeper stretch.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques; Dena Gardiner, Principles of Exercise Therapy; Tidy's Physiotherapy (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) in mechanical ventilation:

options.A: Keeps alveoli open at the end of expiration, improving oxygenation

questions.explanation: PEEP prevents alveolar collapse but may reduce cardiac output and cause barotrauma at high levels.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems; ACSM Guidelines; Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Which fracture is characterised by tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and may be missed on early X-rays?

options.A: Fracture of the first metacarpal base (Bennett)

questions.explanation: Treat as a fracture if suspected clinically; MRI is the best investigation when X-rays are normal.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 4 Orthopedics)
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Clot retraction, which produces a more effective and compact haemostatic plug, is driven by contraction of platelet pseudopodia containing which contractile protein?
questions.explanation: Clot retraction (the fibrin clot contracting to about 40% of its original volume within 5-30 minutes) is produced by contraction of platelet pseudopodia, which contain the contractile actomyosin-like protein historically called thrombosthenin.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: Fibromyalgia is best managed physiotherapeutically with:

options.D: Graded aerobic exercise, education and pacing

questions.explanation: Low-intensity graded aerobic exercise has the best evidence; sleep and stress management are included.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems; ACSM Guidelines; Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Platelets are formed by pinching off bits of cytoplasm from which giant, multinucleated bone marrow cell?
questions.explanation: Platelets are formed within the cytoplasm of the granular megakaryocyte by pinching off bits of cytoplasm, released into circulation when the cell dies — a single megakaryocyte can produce 2,000-4,000 platelets by this process.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: Why can a meniscal injury sometimes present with little or no pain or swelling, making diagnosis more difficult?

options.A: The menisci are avascular and have no nerve supply on their inner two-thirds
options.B: The menisci are the most richly innervated structures in the knee
options.C: Meniscal tears always occur alongside complete ACL rupture, masking symptoms
options.D: Meniscal tissue regenerates immediately after injury

questions.explanation: The menisci are avascular and lack nerve supply on their inner two-thirds, meaning an injury confined to this region can produce little or no pain or swelling — one reason meniscal injury can be difficult to diagnose confidently without a thorough history and examination.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Tests for Meniscus Injury
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Rigor mortis occurs because of:

options.A: Lack of ATP, preventing detachment of myosin heads from actin

questions.explanation: ATP is needed for cross-bridge detachment.
questions.sourceBook: A.K. Jain, Textbook of Physiology; Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology (chapter-level reference)
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: The ratio of the spatial peak intensity to the spatial average intensity of an ultrasound beam is called the:
questions.explanation: BNR describes how evenly power is distributed over the transducer face; a lower BNR (ideally < 6:1) is safer, avoiding hot spots.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: The final descent of the testis into the scrotum during fetal development is mediated primarily by:

options.C: Growth hormone from the fetal pituitary

questions.explanation: While gonadal induction (forming a testis in the first place) is driven by genes on the Y chromosome and initial abdominal migration is guided by the gubernaculum, the final descent of the testis into the scrotum is mediated by testosterone produced by the fetal testis itself.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Genital Development
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: During the remodelling stage of tendon healing, controlled mechanical stress:

options.B: Aligns collagen fibres along the lines of stress and improves tensile strength

questions.explanation: Wolff's law for bone and Davis's law for soft tissue: tissues remodel along the lines of applied force.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Neumann, Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System; Daniels & Worthingham (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 3 Biomechanics)
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: On the International Death Certificate, Part II records:

options.A: The direct/immediate cause of death only
options.B: Other significant conditions that contributed to the death but were not directly related to the disease or condition causing it
options.D: Only conditions unrelated to the patient's death in any way

questions.explanation: Part II of the death certificate records other significant associated conditions that contributed to the death but did not directly lead to it (e.g. diabetes as a contributing but non-causal condition), distinct from Part I, which records the direct cause and the underlying/antecedent causes forming the direct chain to death.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — International Death Certificate
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: A characteristic finding in reaction of degeneration on galvanic testing is:

options.A: Absent response to direct current in all cases
options.B: Cathodal closing contraction much greater than anodal closing contraction with brisk response
options.C: Polarity reversal — anodal closing contraction becomes equal to or greater than cathodal closing contraction

questions.explanation: In normal muscle CCC > ACC with brisk twitches. In RD, contraction is sluggish (vermicular), faradic response is lost and ACC ≥ CCC (polarity reversal).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) is aggravated by:

options.D: Resisted wrist flexion and forearm pronation

questions.explanation: The common flexor/pronator origin is overloaded; resisted wrist flexion reproduces the pain.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: For an effective erythema reaction on skin that has become thickened and pigmented from previous UV exposure, the next dose should be:

options.A: Increased to overcome the protective thickening and tolerance
options.B: Delivered with the lamp at double the distance
options.D: Kept the same, since tolerance never develops

questions.explanation: Repeated exposures produce epidermal thickening (acanthosis) and pigmentation, so tolerance develops and doses must be increased (e.g. by 25–75%) to maintain the same erythema.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Alternating isometric contractions of agonists and antagonists without movement to promote stability is called:
questions.explanation: Rhythmic stabilisation improves co-contraction and stability, e.g. in trunk or weight-bearing control.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: The KT-1000 arthrometer is primarily used to measure which type of knee displacement?

options.A: Anteroposterior displacement of the tibia relative to the femur

questions.explanation: The KT-1000 arthrometer is the most commonly used ligament testing device for the knee, measuring anteroposterior (forward-backward) displacement of the tibia relative to the femur, used to quantify ligamentous laxity (e.g. in ACL/PCL injury) as an adjunct to clinical assessment.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: How does the metabolic response to trauma/sepsis differ from simple starvation regarding ketone formation?

options.A: Both produce identical, unimpaired ketone formation
options.B: In trauma/sepsis, ketone formation is impaired, and glucose-generating protein breakdown cannot be entirely prevented even by giving glucose
options.C: Trauma always increases ketone formation far beyond that seen in starvation
options.D: Ketone formation is irrelevant to both conditions

questions.explanation: Unlike simple starvation (where glucose administration can readily reverse protein catabolism), trauma and sepsis patients have impaired ketone formation, and gluconeogenesis (protein breakdown to make glucose) cannot be entirely prevented by giving exogenous glucose — a key nutritional distinction between the two states.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutrition and Fluid Therapy — Metabolic Response to Trauma and Sepsis
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: In periodized training, the 'competition' phase is generally characterized by:

options.A: Lower loads and the highest number of repetitions and sets
options.B: Higher loads (peaking just prior to competition), with fewer exercises per session and reduced volume compared to the preparation phase
options.D: Only aerobic exercise, no resistance training

questions.explanation: In periodized training, the competition phase uses higher loads peaking just before competition, along with fewer exercises per session and decreased repetitions/sets compared to the earlier preparation phase, which uses lower loads and higher volume.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Periodization and Variation of Training
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Vojta therapy for infants is based on:

options.A: Reflex locomotion elicited through pressure on specific zones

questions.explanation: Reflex creeping and reflex rolling stimulated from trigger zones to activate normal motor patterns.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Per Snyder's classification, a Type II SLAP lesion — described as the most common type — is characterised by:

options.A: A superior labrum that is markedly frayed but with intact attachments
options.B: A small tear with instability of the labral-biceps complex
options.C: A bucket-handle tear that may displace into the joint, with the labral-biceps attachment intact
options.D: A bucket-handle tear extending to the biceps tendon, allowing it to sublux into the joint

questions.explanation: Snyder's classification describes Type I (frayed superior labrum, intact attachments), Type II (small tear with labral-biceps complex instability — the most common type), Type III (bucket-handle tear, labral-biceps attachment intact), and Type IV (bucket-handle tear extending to the biceps tendon, allowing subluxation).
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 5: Shoulder — Tests for Labral Tears, SLAP Classification
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Which modality is CONTRAINDICATED in a patient with haemophilic joint bleeding?

options.A: Shortwave diathermy or deep heat during an acute bleed
options.C: Gentle active movement after bleeding settles

questions.explanation: Heat increases bleeding; use RICE during acute haemarthrosis.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference); standard internal medicine texts
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: In a patellar tendon-bearing (PTB) transtibial prosthesis the main weight-bearing areas are the:

options.A: Patellar tendon and pressure-tolerant areas such as the medial tibial flare
options.B: Head of the fibula and tibial crest
options.D: Distal end of the residual limb

questions.explanation: The PTB socket is relieved over the tibial crest, fibular head and distal end (pressure-intolerant) and loads the patellar tendon and medial tibial flare.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: In a setting with a high local prevalence of C. difficile, why is alcohol gel decontamination between patient contacts considered inadequate?

options.A: Alcohol gel is more effective than hand-washing against C. difficile spores
options.B: Alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores, so hands must be washed with soap and water instead
options.C: C. difficile cannot be transmitted via hands under any circumstances
options.D: Alcohol gel damages skin more than soap and water

questions.explanation: Alcohol gel decontamination is usually adequate for routine hand hygiene, but it does not kill C. difficile spores. In situations of high C. difficile prevalence (e.g. a local outbreak), hands must be washed with soap and water instead, since spores survive alcohol-based decontamination.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Infection Prevention and Control — Health Care-Associated Infection
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: The normal range of hip flexion (knee flexed) is approximately:
questions.explanation: AAOS: hip flexion 0–120°, extension 0–30°, abduction 0–45°, adduction 0–30°, medial/lateral rotation 0–45°.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills
